query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a . The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1 ). An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region. decision.trend: Research has focused on improving the strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys through various processing methods and microstructural design strategies. Earlier studies have explored the effects of conventional processing, alloying additions, and thermal treatments on the mechanical properties of these alloys. More recent studies have investigated the use of advanced processing techniques, such as selective laser melting and spark plasma sintering, to create high-entropy alloys with improved strength and ductility. Additionally, researchers have explored the use of precipitation strengthening and grain refinement to enhance the mechanical properties of these alloys.
decision.unsolved: Despite significant progress, room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility remain major challenges for high-entropy alloys. The development of processing methods and microstructural design strategies that can simultaneously improve strength and ductility while minimizing brittleness is an ongoing area of research.
decision.lever: precipitation strengthening through stepwise thermo-mechanical processes
decision.why: The use of precipitation strengthening through stepwise thermo-mechanical processes has shown promise in improving the strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys. By tailoring the precipitation structures and grain refinement, researchers can create alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility. This approach has been successfully demonstrated in recent studies, such as PMC10213035, and offers a potential solution to the ongoing challenge of room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility in high-entropy alloys.
